transcript.text: Thorndyke’s
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: Good morning.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: Is that Mr Thorndyke?
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: Speaking.
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: How can I help?
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: I’ve got quite a few things which need painting and fixing in the flat and I wonder whether you’d be able to do the work.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: I’m sure I’d be able to help but let me take down a few details.
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: Yes, of course.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: Well, firstly, how did you hear about us?
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: It was my friend May Hampton … you did some excellent work for her a couple of years ago.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: Do you remember?
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: Oh, yes, that was in West Park Flats, lovely lady.
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: Yes, she is.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: And what’s your name, please?
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: It’s Edith Pargetter.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: Edith … can you spell your surname, please?
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: It’s P-A-R-G-E-double T-E-R.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: Double T, right.
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: And do you live in West Park Flats as well?
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: No, actually it’s East Park, Flat 4.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: Oh, right, that’s over the road, I seem to remember – quite difficult to get to.
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: Yes, it’s at the back of the library.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: Right, I know.
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: And what’s your phone number?
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: 875934 but I’m out a great deal in the afternoons and evenings.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: So would the best time to ring you be in the morning?
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: Fine.
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: I’ve made a note of that.
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: Can I just ask, I’ll be in a van and I know parking’s rather difficult round your flats.
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: Where would you recommend?
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: Well, I always tell people in larger vehicles to park by the postbox on the other side of the road from the entrance.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: Good, thanks.
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: And will you be able to give me a full itemised quote?
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: Oh, yes, I’ll list all the jobs separately with individual prices.
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: That’d be a great help.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: No problem.
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: Now, what would you like me to do?
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: Firstly and most urgently is in the kitchen.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: With all the weather damage, the glass in the door has cracked and I’d need that fixing …
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: I presume you mean replacing?
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: Oh, yes.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: And as soon as possible …
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: What I’ll do is come round tomorrow morning and do that immediately.
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: Thank you so much.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: The other things aren’t so urgent but …
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: Now, I’ll make a note of everything you want doing.
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: Well, in the kitchen I’d like some painting doing.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: All the kitchen walls?
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: Just the area over the cooker.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: It’s very greasy …
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: Right … it does tend to get that way!
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: Yes!
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: Well, if you want a proper job done what I’d need to do is strip the old paint and plaster it about a week before I paint it.
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: Of course.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: Now, May tells me you also do work in the garden.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: Well, I’d like you to replace a fence.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: Just one?
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: Yes, at the far end.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: Fine.
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: Shouldn’t be a problem.
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: And that’s the lot.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: Fine.
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: Yeah, as I say I can come round tomorrow morning to look over things with you.
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: That’s great, thank you.
transcript.speaker: EDITH

transcript.text: So, I’ll look forward to seeing you tomorrow at …
transcript.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

transcript.text: Welcome to Manham Port, where a thousand years of history are brought to life.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: All the family can enjoy a day out at Manham: visit our copper mine, see models of the machinery it used, have your photo taken in nineteenth-century costume, experience at first hand how people lived at different stages throughout history, and especially how children studied, worked and played.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The port of Manham is located in beautiful and peaceful countryside, on a bend in the great River Avon, and developed here because it’s the highest navigable point of the Avon – boats can go no higher up this river – and proved a handy place to load and unload cargo to and from the sea, which is over 23 miles away.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: A small port was already established here when, about 900 years ago, tin was discovered nearby, though it wasn’t until the Industrial Revolution, when a tremendous need for metals of all kinds developed, that Manham expanded to become one of the busiest ports in the country.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: And because it was already so busy, prospectors began to look for other minerals, and by the end of the nineteenth century, lead, copper, manganese and arsenic were added to the cargos leaving Manham.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: In the early days, the ores had been smelted – or processed – in the same area they were mined.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: But, as demand grew, the smelting process required huge factory furnaces or fires to melt the metal from the rock and there was not enough coal in the local area, so the rocks containing minerals had to be shipped long distances.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Sadly, in the twentieth century, the great port of Manham declined, and thousands of workers were forced to emigrate out of the area.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The building at the port fell into disrepair, and the place became almost forgotten.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: But then, the Manham Trust was formed to conserve the historical resources of the area.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It organised scores of local volunteers to remove undergrowth to find the original outlines of the installations.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It then brought in paid professionals to match installations with maps of the original port complex and to set about reconstructing it.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Today you can see the results of this ambitious programme of restoration.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The intention, and we believe this will be realised before the end of the year, is to return Manham Port to the condition it reached at its peak as ‘the greatest copper port in the country’.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: But what can you do and see on your visit today?
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Here are just a few highlights.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We suggest you start with the visit to the copper mine.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Travel on converted mining trains and journey into the depths of the mountain along seams once worked by hundreds of miners.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Watch out especially for the great pumping machines which rid the mine of water.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: But please be warned that, like all mines, ours is very dark and closed in and we do say that children under five and also dogs should NOT be taken into the mine.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The next recommended visit is to the village school.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: While looking round the classrooms, take a special look at our display of games, which is one of the largest in the world.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: And it’s recommended that you time your visit to coincide with a guided tour.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: This will give you the opportunity to ask lots of questions.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Near the school is the beautiful old sailing ketch called ‘The George’.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: You are welcome to board the boat and look round the cabins.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Look out for the shop’s wheel which was missing until only five years ago when it was dredged out of the silt by a local fisherman.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We have no idea how it got there but it’s been polished and proudly restored to its original place on the boat.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Please take care going down the ladders if you wish to visit the lower deck – we don’t recommend you allow young children to use them.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: So we hope you have a memorable visit to Manham Port and will tell your friends all about us.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Hi, Laura – could you spare a few minutes to talk about the work placement you did last summer?
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: I’m thinking of doing one myself …
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: Hi, Tim.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: Sure.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: Didn’t you do yours at an environmental services company?
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: That’s right … It’s only a very small company and they needed someone to produce a company brochure, and I wanted to get some business experience because I’m interested in a career in occupational psychology in a business environment.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: It was good because I had overall responsibility for the project.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: What kind of skills do you think you developed on the placement?
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: I mean, apart from the ones you already had … Did you have to do all the artwork for the brochure, the layout and everything?
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: We hired the services of a professional photographer for that.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: I did have to use my IT skills to a certain extent because I cut and pasted text from marketing leaflets, but that didn’t involve anything I hadn’t done before.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: Do you think you got any better at managing your time and prioritizing things?
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: You always used to say you had trouble with that …
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: Oh, definitely.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: There was so much pressure to meet the project deadline.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: And I also got better at explaining things and asserting my opinions, because I had to have weekly consultations with the marketing manager and give him a progress report.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: It sounds as if you got a lot out of it then.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: Absolutely.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: It was really worthwhile … But you know, the company benefited too …
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: Yes, they must have done.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: After all, if they’d used a professional advertising agency to produce their brochure instead of doing it in-house, presumably they’d have paid a lot more?
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: Oh, yes.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: I worked it out – it would have been 250 per cent more.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: And I thought the end result was good, even though we did everything on site.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: The company has quite a powerful computer and I managed to borrow some scanning software from the university.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: The new brochure looks really professional; it enhances the image of the company straight away.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: So in the long run it should help them to attract clients, and improve their sales figures?
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: That’s the idea.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: Yeah.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: Well, all in all it sounds very positive – I think I will go ahead and apply for a placement myself.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: How do I go about it?
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: It’s easy enough to do, because there’s a government agency called STEP – S-T-E-P – that organises placements for students.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: You should start by getting their booklet with all the details – I expect you can download one from their website.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: Actually, they’ve got copies in the psychology department – I’ve seen them there.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: I’ll just go to the office and pick one up.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: And then if I were you, after I’d looked at it I’d go over all the options with someone …
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: I suppose I should ask my tutor’s advice.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: He knows more about me than anyone.
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: One of the career officers would be better, they’ve got more knowledge about the jobs market than your personal tutor would have.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: OK …
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: And then when you know what you want you can register with STEP – you’ll find their address in the booklet.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: And once you’ve registered they assign you to a mentor who looks after your application.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: And then I suppose you just sit back and wait till you hear something?
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: They told me at the careers office that it’s best to be proactive, and get updates yourself by checking the website for new placement alerts.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: Your mentor is supposed to keep you informed, but you can’t rely on that.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: I don’t suppose it’s a good idea to get in touch with companies directly, is it?
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: Not really … But it is the company who notifies you if they want you to go for an interview.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: You get a letter of invitation or an email from personnel departments.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: And do I reply directly to them?
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: Yes, you do.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: STEP only gets involved again once you’ve been made a job offer.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: Right … So, once you’ve had an interview you should let your mentor know what the outcome is?
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: I mean whether you’re offered a job, and whether you’ve decided to accept it?
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: They’ll inform the careers office once a placement has been agreed, so you don’t have to do that.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: Is that all then?
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: More or less.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: Only once you’ve accepted an offer you’ll probably have to supply a reference, because the placement will be conditional on that.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: And that’s something you should ask your own tutor to provide.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: He knows about your academic ability and also about your qualities, like reliability.
transcript.speaker: LAURA

transcript.text: Well, thanks very much for the information – I’m starting to look forward …
transcript.speaker: TIM

transcript.text: Today we’re going to look at an important area of science, namely nanotechnology.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So what is it?
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Nano means tiny, so it’s science and engineering on the scale of atoms and molecules.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The idea is that by controlling and rearranging atoms, you can literally create anything.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: However, as we’ll see, the science of the small has some big implications affecting us in many ways.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: There’s no doubt that nanotechnology promises so much for civilisation.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: However, all new technologies have their teething problems.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And with nanotechnology, society often gets the wrong idea about its capabilities.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Numerous science-fiction books and movies have raised people’s fears about nanotechnology – with scenarios such as inserting little nano-robots into your body that monitor everything you do without you realising it, or self-replicating nano-robots that eventually take over the world.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So how do we safeguard such a potentially powerful technology?
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Some scientists recommend that nano-particles be treated as new chemicals with separate safety tests and clear labelling.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: They believe that greater care should also be taken with nano-particles in laboratories and factories.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Others have called for a withdrawal of new nano products such as cosmetics and a temporary halt to many kinds of nanotech research.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But as far as I’m concerned there’s a need to plough ahead with the discoveries and applications of nanotechnology.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: I really believe that most scientists would welcome a way to guard against unethical uses of such technology.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: We can’t go around thinking that all innovation is bad, all advancement is bad.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: As with the debate about any new technology, it is how you use it that’s important.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So let’s look at some of its possible uses.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Thanks to nanotechnology, there could be a major breakthrough in the field of transportation with the production of more durable metals.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: These could be virtually unbreakable, lighter and much more pliable leading to planes that are 50 times lighter than at present.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Those same improved capabilities will dramatically reduce the cost of travelling into space making it more accessible to ordinary people and opening up a totally new holiday destination.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In terms of technology, the computer industry will be able to shrink computer parts down to minute sizes.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: We need nanotechnology in order to create a new generation of computers that will work even faster and will have a million times more memory but will be about the size of a sugar cube.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Nanotechnology could also revolutionise the way that we generate power.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The cost of solar cells will be drastically reduced so harnessing this energy will be far more economical than at present.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But nanotechnology has much wider applications than this and could have an enormous impact on our environment.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For instance, tiny airborne nano-robots could be programmed to actually rebuild the ozone layer, which could lessen the impact of global warming on our planet.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: That’s a pretty amazing thought, isn’t it?
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: On a more local scale, this new technology could help with the clean-up of environmental disasters as nanotechnology will allow us to remove oil and other contaminants from the water far more effectively.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And, if nanotechnology progresses as expected – as a sort of building block set of about 90 atoms – then you could build anything you wanted from the bottom up.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In terms of production, this means that you only use what you need and so there wouldn’t be any waste.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The notion that you could create anything at all has major implications for our health.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It means that we’ll eventually be able to replicate anything.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This would have a phenomenal effect on our society.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In time it could even lead to the eradication of famine through the introduction of machines that produce food to feed the hungry.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But it’s in the area of medicine that nanotechnology may have its biggest impact.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: How we detect disease will change as tiny biosensors are developed to analyse tests in minutes rather than days.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: There’s even speculation nano-robots could be used to slow the ageing process, lengthening life expectancy.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: As you can see, I’m very excited by the implications that could be available to us in the next few decades.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Just how long it’ll take, I honestly don’t know.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER
